.title: Trading Order Blocks *the right way*
.yt_title: Trading Order Blocks the Right Way – Find, Rate, Entry & Stop on Gold (XAUUSD)
.chapters[0].title: Trading Order Blocks the right way
.chapters[0].segs[0].say: Almost everyone has heard of order blocks. But most traders just mark any random candle – and then wonder why price cuts straight through it. The difference is in the details.
.chapters[0].segs[1].say: In this video you'll learn how to find an order block, how to rate its quality, where a sensible entry is – and where your stop belongs.
.chapters[0].segs[2].say: Important up front: this is educational content, not investment advice. Trading involves risk of loss. Practise new strategies on a demo account first.
.chapters[1].title: What is an *order block*?
.chapters[1].hook: What is an order block? Explained simply
.chapters[1].segs[0].say: An order block is a price zone where large market participants have likely placed a lot of orders. On the chart, it's easy to spot.
.chapters[1].segs[2].say: Then the market turns up with a powerful impulse. A move like that rarely happens by chance.
.chapters[1].segs[3].say: The last red candle before this impulse is the bullish order block. This is where buying started – and there are often still orders waiting there.
.chapters[1].segs[4].say: Later, price comes back into exactly this zone. That's called the test, or mitigation, of the order block.
.chapters[1].segs[5].say: And here the market reacts higher again. A bearish order block is the mirror image: the last green candle before a strong sell-off.
.chapters[2].title: Finding *order blocks*
.chapters[2].hook: How to find a real order block
.chapters[2].segs[0].say: Not every red candle is an order block. For a zone to count, something important has to happen afterwards. Let's go through it step by step.
.chapters[2].segs[1].say: The market is in a downtrend. Note the last lower high – that's the line that has to be broken later.
.chapters[2].segs[2].say: Then comes the last red candle before the buyers take over. That's our candidate.
.chapters[2].segs[3].say: Now the first condition: the impulse breaks above the last lower high. Only this break of structure turns the candle into a real order block.
.chapters[2].segs[4].say: The second condition: the impulse is so fast that it leaves a Fair Value Gap behind. That shows how strong the buyers were.
.chapters[2].segs[5].say: Now the zone is marked: from the low to the high of the last red candle.
.chapters[2].segs[6].say: On the pullback, price tests the zone and turns higher again. Without the break of structure and without the gap, it would have been just an ordinary candle.
.chapters[3].title: Rating *order blocks*
.chapters[3].hook: Strong or weak order block? 5 criteria
.chapters[3].segs[0].say: There are plenty of order blocks. The question is: which ones are worth trading? For that we use five criteria.
.chapters[3].segs[1].say: Here gold first forms a low. Stops are sitting below it.
.chapters[3].segs[2].say: The last red candle wicks below this low and grabs the liquidity. An order block with a sweep is much stronger.
.chapters[3].segs[3].say: Then the impulse breaks above the last high. A clear break of structure.
.chapters[3].segs[4].say: And it leaves a Fair Value Gap right above the zone.
.chapters[3].segs[5].say: The order block also sits below the fifty percent level of the whole move – in other words, in discount. For buys, that's the cheaper area.
.chapters[3].segs[6].say: And finally: the zone is still untouched. An order block that has already been tested several times usually has few open orders left.
.chapters[4].title: The *entry*
.chapters[4].hook: 3 ways to trade an order block
.chapters[4].segs[0].say: You've found a good order block. Now it's about the entry. There are three common approaches – each with pros and cons.
.chapters[4].segs[1].say: Here's our zone, formed before a powerful impulse.
.chapters[4].segs[2].say: Price pulls back. Option one: a limit order at the top edge of the order block. You're very likely to get filled, but your stop is the furthest away.
.chapters[4].segs[3].say: Option two: you wait for the middle of the zone, the fifty percent level. Your stop gets tighter, but sometimes the order doesn't get filled.
.chapters[4].segs[4].say: In this example the wick reaches exactly the middle and the entry is triggered.
.chapters[4].segs[5].say: Option three: you wait until price shows a reaction inside the zone – for example a Change of Character on the lower timeframe. It costs you a bit of price, but it filters out a lot of failed attempts.
.chapters[4].segs[6].say: Which option fits depends on your style. What matters is that you decide in advance – not in the heat of the moment.
.chapters[5].title: Stop & *target*
.chapters[5].hook: Where does the stop go on an order block?
.chapters[5].segs[0].say: The entry is only half the job. Just as important is where your stop sits and where your target is.
.chapters[5].segs[1].say: Once again we have an order block after a strong impulse.
.chapters[5].segs[2].say: Price comes back and the entry is taken inside the zone.
.chapters[5].segs[3].say: The stop goes below the low of the order block, with a little buffer. Gold often prints long wicks – a stop right at the edge gets taken out quickly.
.chapters[5].segs[4].say: A good target is the next pool of liquidity, here the old high. Before entering, check whether the distance to the target is actually worth it compared to the stop.
.chapters[5].segs[5].say: In this example price runs above the high. But the same rule applies: if a candle closes clearly below the order block, the zone is invalid. Then the stop does its job – no discussion.
.chapters[6].title: Remember *this*
.chapters[6].segs[1].say: An order block is valid as long as price reacts at the zone.
.chapters[6].segs[2].say: If a candle closes clearly below it, it's invalid – and you're out.
.chapters[7].title: The *summary*
.chapters[7].segs[1].say: A bullish order block is the last red candle before a strong impulse higher.
.chapters[7].segs[1].bullet: Last red candle before the impulse
.chapters[7].segs[2].say: It only counts if the impulse breaks structure and leaves a Fair Value Gap.
.chapters[7].segs[3].say: The strongest zones have taken liquidity first, sit in discount and are still untouched.
.chapters[7].segs[4].say: Decide on your entry in advance: top edge, middle or confirmation.
.chapters[7].segs[5].say: The stop goes below the zone. And risk only one to two percent of your account per trade.
